This reign's own end had not previously been documented.

title: iiwf-world-heavyweight
label: Subway Psycho

won.source: The Subway Psycho defeats "Outlaw" J.W. Hardin for the World Heavyweight Championship at the original Ring Wars, 29 June 1996, per a Classics re-broadcast of the match with an explicit dateline (msg_id ONqZtaAIxqYJ, served under this wing).

lost.source: Accused of vandalizing the New York subway system, the Psycho is stripped of the title -- not pinned -- "which then fell into the hands of Deathbringer," per a biographical retrospective (msg_id RkO35zqJ6LUJ, served under this wing). No exact stripping date survives in this pass's own reading; the reign ends sometime before Deathbringer's own tenure and well before Otto Verhoeven's 12 October 1996 Casket Match win (r03, now dated by this same pass).

note: A previously entirely unrecorded reign, inserted into the held record's title chain between "Outlaw" J.W. Hardin (r01) and Deathbringer (r02); the Psycho was later cleared of the vandalism charges and granted the key to the city of New York, per the same retrospective, but the title itself was never restored to him.

won.source: Otto Verhoeven defeats Deathbringer in a Casket Match at Ring Wars II to win the World Heavyweight Championship, per a Classics re-broadcast recap naming the match (msg_id YU7YNiln5hkJ, served under this wing); a second Classics episode independently dates Ring Wars II itself to 12 October 1996 (msg_id RZAWIRGkW0kJ, served under this wing). This dates and sources the reign for the first time; it had previously been visible only in the fed's own weekly rankings table.

lost.source: Dan "Flash" Kauffman, substituting for an injured Chris Quigley, defeats Otto "the Butcher" Verhoeven for the World Heavyweight Championship in a screwjob finish, per a Classics re-broadcast's own host narration (msg_id OGTr4HtOejgJ, served under this wing), which attests the method and the substitution but gives no exact date for the title match itself (distinct from the earlier match the episode actually re-broadcasts, a September 1996 Coronation Clash Tournament bout between Quigley and Verhoeven). This reign's own end had not previously been documented; the loss is bounded before r04's own earliest sighting (15 November 1996).

lost.source: Casey "Blackheart" James's title defense against "Lone Wolf" Brody Thunder on IIWF Saturday Night ends in a disputed double-pin; the acting IIWF President rules the match a draw and, citing James's own pattern of controversial finishes, strips him of the title on the spot, per the fed's own broadcast (msg_id yVTonN13RAAJ, served under this wing). The held record's reign record had previously left this reign's own end completely undocumented.

note: Vacated for the Coronation Clash II tournament, June-July 1997.

No results report for the show itself survives in the held record; the December 1998 billing already on file (outside this wing's own pre-read) is consistent with an unbroken reign from this date.

note: This pass dates the win to the announced 1 August 1998 IIWF Forever Eternal Rumble and confirms it via the champion's own November roleplay, closing the chain between Thunder's prior reign and the December 1998 billing already on file. No title-loss document survives in the held record, so `lost` is left unset.

won.source: ERRATUM CORRECTED: the previously-cited date and source do not survive scrutiny. The cited document (msg_id zks8f84PxncJ, a Monday Musings column dated two days after the claimed win) instead shows Requiem still champion on 20 September, publicly announcing he is quitting Genesis after retaining the title against "Sychosys" Joe Petrow that same night (see iiwf-intercontinental-r09's own corrected Hour Two citation, same broadcast) -- no title change is shown or claimed anywhere in that document. "The Triple Cross" is an unrelated epithet for Brody Thunder, first seen at Ring Wars IV (8 November 1997, msg_id Bt7Q6x6OGhMJ, not served under this wing), not a dated event. This pass's own reading instead finds the actual title match -- Requiem [c] vs. "Lone Wolf" Brody Thunder -- opening on IIWF Saturday Night, 4 October 1997 (msg_id uzmeMkXL4xQJ, served under this wing; lead-in at msg_id n3VDCBezuBMJ, served under this wing), the first primary-source sighting of this title change. The surviving record does not carry this broadcast's own remaining parts, so the finish itself is not recovered; the win is therefore bounded no earlier than 4 October 1997 and no later than 8 November 1997 (Ring Wars IV, where Thunder is already champion). Still billed as reigning champion at the Second Annual Golden Grapple Awards, 22 November 1997 (served under this wing, msg_ids iW-VEdvXCN8J et al.), successfully defended against "Outlaw" J.W. Hardin at Ring Wars IV, 8 November 1997, per the fed's own broadcast (msg_id uLPaM8-M4_EJ, served under this wing; also recapped at msg_id 2YRX93Cx0QYJ, served under this wing), and through December 1997.

title: iiwf-world-heavyweight

title: iiwf-intercontinental

note: The won.source field is corrected accordingly.

title: iiwf-us-tag-team
label: Prophets of Rage

won.source: The Prophets of Rage defeat the Harlequins for the United States Tag Team Championship, aided by a misguided assist from a broadcaster at ringside, per the fed's own dirt-sheet column reporting the previous night's card (msg_id iYV3eohQlUsJ, served under this wing), which also confirms the Prophets as "the third team to hold the titles in just over a month" since the belt's own introduction at Ring Wars III (22 March 1997). This corrects and dates the reign for the first time; the previously-cited 2 May 1997 date and uncited result-receipt source do not survive independent corroboration in this pass's own reading.

note: Billed as "the defunct IIWF United States Tag Team Championship" in the Golden Grapple Awards stage direction, 22 November 1997 (served under this wing); no formal retirement announcement survives in the held record.

title: iiwf-world-tag-team
label: High Plains Drifters

won.source: No winning receipt survives in the held record; the Drifters are already champions when a Classics re-broadcast picks them up on 26 August 1996 (msg_id v0PyT575yuAJ, served under this wing).

lost.source: The Armed Forces (NavCom and DefCon) defeat the High Plains Drifters (Pale Rider and Easy Rider) for the World Tag Team Championship, aided by manager Aaron the Caddy's own interference, per a Classics re-broadcast of the match with an explicit dateline (msg_id v0PyT575yuAJ, served under this wing).

note: A previously entirely unrecorded reign, and the Drifters' own first documented holding period of this title -- distinct from their own later, already-recorded second reign (r03, visible as champions 26 December 1996), which this reign predates by four months with the Armed Forces and Rising Sun Revolution (r02, visible 22 October 1996) holding the belts in between. The record describes the ending as: manager interference.

title: iiwf-world-heavyweight
label: Serge Annis

won.source: Not dated in this collection's own holdings; Annis is already champion when this pass's own corpus reading picks him up.

lost.source: The fed's own 13 July 1998 IIWF Forever card announcement (msg_id WeO8SjeqlWMJ, served under this wing) bills "Serge Annis surrenders the IIWF World Heavyweight Championship" as a stipulation of the show, vacating the title for the Eternal Rumble.

note: Fills the gap between Requiem's reign (won 12 July 1997, r06) and "Sychosys" Joe Petrow's reign; Annis's own win over the prior champion is not documented in the held record.
